why_how.text: Turns put you across other people's paths, so careful checks and a steady plan prevent crashes.
Left turns carry a special risk from both oncoming traffic and rear-end hits.

scenario.text: Mia waits halfway into an intersection to turn left with her wheels already turned left.

reasoning.text: If she is hit from behind, turned wheels would push her into oncoming traffic, so the wheels stay straight while waiting.

result.text: Mia straightens her wheels and turns only when the path is clear.

claim.text: Common mistake: turning the wheels left early while waiting, to be ready to go.

correction.text: Keep the steering wheel and wheels straight while waiting, so a rear-end hit does not push you into oncoming traffic.

prompt.text: You are waiting to turn left and a car is approaching fast from behind. Where should your wheels point?

rationale.text: Straight wheels keep a rear-end hit from pushing you into oncoming traffic while you wait to turn.

narration.text: This lesson begins the second part of the basics with turning, something you will do on nearly every drive. You will learn the checks to make before any turn, why last-second changes of plan cause crashes, how to stay in your own lane while giving large vehicles the room they need, and how to set up a left turn at an intersection. The lesson ends with one small habit that matters a great deal while you wait to turn left. These rules show up both on the knowledge test and on the skills test, where every turn you make is graded.

Before any turn, check your mirrors, your surroundings and your blind spot, stay in your lane, signal your turn and yield the right-of-way. Plan your turns early. Last-second changes of plan are unsafe and can cause a crash, so check your mirrors and the traffic behind you before turning into a side road or driveway. A driver who suddenly brakes and swerves into a driveway gives the car behind no warning at all. If you realize too late that you have reached your turn, it is safer to continue and come back than to force the turn at the last moment.

lines.text: Do not cut the center line.
Give trucks and buses extra room.

narration.text: Do not change lanes in the middle of a turn or cut across the center line. Finish the turn in the lane you started toward. Leave extra room for trucks and buses, which may swing over the center line as they turn. That creates an easy trap: seeing a bus cross the line, a driver may think it is acceptable to do the same. It is not. Large vehicles swing wide because of their length, while your car can make the turn within its lane. So when a big vehicle is turning near you, hold back and give it space rather than copying its path.

lines.text: Clear path; keep near the center line.
Watch for pedestrians on the left.

narration.text: For a left turn, check that your path is clear and keep near the center line. Watch for pedestrians crossing on the left, who are easy to miss while you are watching oncoming cars. Wait about halfway into the intersection while leaving room for oncoming drivers who are also turning left. From that position you can see oncoming traffic clearly and complete the turn quickly when a gap opens. Do not start the turn until both the oncoming lanes and the crosswalk you will drive through are clear, and take your time if you are unsure.

lines.text: Turned wheels plus a rear hit: danger.
Keep the wheels straight until you go.

narration.text: Here is the trap. While waiting to turn left, many drivers turn the steering wheel early so they are ready to go. The handbook says to keep the steering wheel and wheels straight instead, because if you are hit from behind with the wheel turned left, you will be pushed into oncoming traffic. With straight wheels, a rear-end hit pushes you forward rather than across the path of approaching cars. It feels slower, but turning the wheel takes only a moment once the path is clear, and it removes one of the most dangerous outcomes at a busy intersection.

Here is a quick check: you are waiting to turn left, and a car is approaching fast from behind. Where should your wheels point? Think about what a rear-end hit would do. The answer is straight ahead. Straight wheels keep a rear-end hit from pushing you into oncoming traffic while you wait to turn. You should already be about halfway into the intersection, near the center line, watching for pedestrians on the left. Once the path is clear, turn the wheel and complete the turn into the correct lane without cutting across the center line.

lines.text: Check, stay in lane, signal, yield.

narration.text: To wrap up: before any turn, check your mirrors, surroundings and blind spot, stay in your lane, signal and yield. Avoid last-second changes of plan, and check behind you before turning into a side road or driveway. Never change lanes mid-turn or cut across the center line, and give trucks and buses extra room because they may swing over it. For a left turn, keep near the center line, watch for pedestrians, and wait about halfway into the intersection with your wheels straight. Next you will learn the rules for turning around: U-turns and Y-turns.

why_how.text: Turning around and choosing turn lanes correctly keeps you out of other drivers' paths.
The Y-turn is a skills test maneuver, so its steps are worth learning exactly.

scenario.text: Leo needs to turn around on a narrow residential street too tight for a U-turn.

reasoning.text: A Y-turn is the maneuver for that street: right, left across, back, then forward.

result.text: Leo completes the Y-turn, reversing only on the third step.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a U-turn is never allowed outside a marked intersection.

correction.text: On any rural two-lane highway a U-turn is allowed as long as it is done safely and does not interfere with traffic.

prompt.text: During a Y-turn, at which step do you first look back over your right shoulder?

rationale.text: Step three is the only reversing step: look back over your right shoulder and back up just far enough to drive forward.

lines.text: U-turns and where they are allowed.

narration.text: This lesson covers turning around and choosing the right lane for a turn. You will learn what a U-turn is, how to check before making one, and where it is allowed. Then you will see how to handle multiple turn lanes and right turns on a four-lane road. Finally, the lesson walks through the Y-turn step by step. The Y-turn deserves extra attention because you will be asked to perform one on the driving exam, so knowing the order of its steps is useful on both the knowledge test and the skills test. Learning both the U-turn and the Y-turn properly pays off twice.

A U-turn is one smooth U-shaped motion that reverses your direction. It can be very dangerous even though some intersections allow it, because you cross every lane of traffic in a single sweep. Before a U-turn, check all mirrors and traffic and look for any sign that prohibits it. On any rural two-lane highway a U-turn is allowed as long as it is done safely and does not interfere with traffic. So the questions to ask are always the same: is there a sign forbidding it, is traffic clear in both directions, and can you finish it without making anyone slow down.

lines.text: Multiple lanes: end in the matching lane.
Four-lane road: turn right from the curb lane.

narration.text: With multiple turn lanes, finish the turn in the matching lane. If you start in the left-most lane, end in the left-most lane; if you start in the middle, end in the middle. That way drivers turning beside you never cross your path. When turning right from a four-lane roadway, the turn must be made from the lane closest to the right curb or road edge. Moving into the correct lane early, well before the intersection, makes both rules easy to follow and avoids a sudden lane change in the last few car lengths before the turn.

lines.text: Residential streets too narrow for a U-turn.
Also asked for on the driving exam.

narration.text: Use a Y-turn only in residential areas on streets too narrow for a U-turn. You will also be asked to perform one on the driving exam, so practice it before test day. Unlike the U-turn, a Y-turn is a stop-and-reverse turnaround made in separate steps. Choose a quiet stretch of street with good visibility in both directions, away from driveways where cars might back out and away from hills or curves that hide oncoming traffic. Then follow the four steps in order, checking traffic at each one, so the maneuver stays slow and controlled.

lines.text: One: signal right, pull right, stop.
Three: back up. Four: pull forward.

narration.text: Step one: signal right, check your mirrors and the traffic on your right, move over as far to the right as possible, and stop. Step two: signal left, check your blind spot, turn left across to the opposite curb and stop. Step three: look back over your right shoulder and reverse just far enough to drive forward again, then stop. Step four: check left and right and pull forward into your lane. Each step ends with a stop, which gives you a moment to check traffic again before the next part of the turn, and keeps the whole maneuver slow.

Here is the trap: two turnarounds with similar names. A U-turn is a single continuous motion and is allowed on any rural two-lane highway when safe, unless a sign forbids it. A Y-turn is a stop-and-reverse turnaround reserved for residential streets too narrow for a U-turn, and it is also a graded maneuver on the driving exam. A question that mentions backing up is describing a Y-turn; one that describes a single smooth sweep is a U-turn. Match the street too: narrow residential streets call for the Y-turn, open rural two-lane highways allow a safe U-turn.

lines.text: Y-turn: when do you look back?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: during a Y-turn, at which step do you first look back over your right shoulder? Walk through the steps in order. The answer is the third step, before reversing. Step three is the only reversing step: you look back over your right shoulder and back up just far enough to drive forward again, then stop. Steps one and two move you to the right curb and then across to the opposite curb, and step four checks left and right before you pull forward into your lane to finish the turnaround. The order matters on test day.

In summary: a U-turn is one smooth motion that can be very dangerous; check mirrors, traffic and signs first, and remember it is allowed on any rural two-lane highway when safe and not interfering with traffic. With multiple turn lanes, finish in the matching lane, and turn right from the curb lane on a four-lane road. Use a Y-turn only on residential streets too narrow for a U-turn: signal right and stop, signal left and cross, look back and reverse, then pull forward. Next you will learn the rules for passing and changing lanes.

why_how.text: Passing and lane changes put you beside other vehicles at speed, where blind spots and misjudged gaps cause crashes.
Clear rules for where and how to pass keep the move predictable.

scenario.text: Ivy passes a slow car and starts moving back as soon as her rear bumper clears its front.

reasoning.text: The safe cue is seeing both headlights of the passed car in the rearview mirror.

result.text: Ivy waits until both headlights show, then signals and returns.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking mirrors are enough before changing lanes.

correction.text: Blind spots are seen only by looking over the shoulder toward the new lane.

memory_support.text: Signal, shoulder check, one lane, both headlights back.

prompt.text: Traffic ahead is stopped for a car waiting to turn left. May you use the paved shoulder to get around it?

answer.text: Yes; the shoulder may be used to get around a stopped or left-turning vehicle.

rationale.text: The shoulder is allowed only past a stopped or left-turning vehicle; normal passing uses the left lane.

lines.text: How to change lanes and return.

narration.text: This lesson covers passing and changing lanes, two moves that put you right beside other vehicles at speed. You will learn when a paved shoulder may be used, which lane is for going around slower traffic, and what to do when someone passes you. Then the lesson covers the checks for any lane change, including blind spots, and the rules for passing safely: how many vehicles, which side, how fast, how much room, and the clear cue for when it is safe to move back. Each rule here is short, but together they prevent many crashes.

lines.text: Shoulder: only past stopped or left-turners.
Passing on the right is risky.

narration.text: You may use a paved shoulder to get around a vehicle only when that vehicle is stopped or is making a left turn. Otherwise the shoulder is not a travel lane. On a multi-lane road the left-most lane is the lane for going around slower vehicles. Passing on the right is risky because the other driver may not see you there, especially if they decide to move right. If another driver is trying to pass you, keep to your lane and slow down so they can complete the pass quickly and safely, rather than speeding up and making the pass longer.

lines.text: Make sure the way is clear.
Signal first; one lane at a time.

narration.text: Before changing lanes, make sure the way is clear, signal first, move only one lane at a time, and look over the shoulder on the side you are moving toward. The areas you check over your left and right shoulders are blind spots, which cannot be seen by using your mirrors alone. A car can sit in your blind spot for a long time without appearing in any mirror. Crossing several lanes at once multiplies the risk, so if you need to move over more than one lane, signal and move one lane, check again, and then move the next.

lines.text: Shoulder check toward the new lane.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Drivers who check every mirror carefully may feel ready to change lanes. But checking mirrors is not enough, because the blind spots are seen only by looking over the shoulder toward the new lane. The quick turn of the head is the step that catches the car beside your rear door. Make the order a habit: mirrors, signal, shoulder check, then move. Lane changes are one of the graded skills on the road test, and on any road that head check is the difference between a smooth move and a sideswipe. Make the head check automatic.

lines.text: One vehicle at a time, on the left.
Room ahead; nobody must move over.

narration.text: Pass only one vehicle at a time and only on the left, since there may not be time to get around several vehicles or even the one ahead of you. Do not linger in the passing lane, and never exceed the speed limit to complete a pass. Pass only when there is enough room in front of the vehicle you are passing, and remember that other drivers are not required to move over for you. If you would need to speed or squeeze back in to finish, the pass is not safe, so stay behind and wait for a better opportunity. Patience is part of every safe pass.

lines.text: Both headlights in your rearview mirror.

narration.text: It is safe to return to the driving lane once both headlights of the vehicle you passed appear in your rearview mirror. That simple cue tells you there is enough space between your rear bumper and the front of the other vehicle. Moving back as soon as you are past its front bumper is too soon and forces the other driver to brake. When both headlights show, signal, check your blind spot again, and move back smoothly. Then return to your normal speed so the driver you passed is not left closing the gap behind you. That cue works on every kind of road.

lines.text: Car stopped to turn left: shoulder?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: traffic ahead is stopped behind a car waiting to turn left. May you use the paved shoulder to get around it? Think about the two cases the handbook allows. The answer is yes. You may use a paved shoulder to get around a vehicle only when it is stopped or making a left turn. Normal passing uses the left-most lane on a multi-lane road, and passing on the right is risky. Even when the shoulder is allowed, move slowly and watch for pedestrians, bicyclists and the turning driver. Use the shoulder only in those two cases.

lines.text: Pass left, one vehicle, within the limit.

narration.text: To sum up: use a paved shoulder only to get around a stopped or left-turning vehicle. The left-most lane is for passing, and passing on the right is risky. When someone passes you, keep your lane and slow down. Before changing lanes, make sure it is clear, signal, move one lane at a time and check your blind spot over your shoulder. Pass one vehicle at a time on the left, never linger or exceed the limit, and pass only with room ahead. Return once both headlights of the passed vehicle appear in your mirror. Passing well is about patience and checks.

why_how.text: Backing is risky because you cannot see well behind a vehicle, so the rules keep it short and slow.
Parking rules keep your car from becoming a hazard, and hill parking keeps it from rolling.

scenario.text: Zoe parks downhill next to a curb and turns her wheels to the left.

reasoning.text: Downhill parking turns the wheels all the way to the right, and the emergency brake is set on any hill.

result.text: Zoe turns the wheels right and sets the emergency brake.

claim.text: Common mistake: backing up on the road after missing an exit.

correction.text: Never back up for a missed exit or turn; continue to the next exit and come back.

memory_support.text: Uphill with a curb, wheels left; otherwise right.

prompt.text: You park uphill on a road with no curb. Which way do the wheels turn?

answer.text: All the way to the right.

rationale.text: Uphill with a curb is the only left-wheel case; uphill without a curb and every downhill park turn right.

lines.text: Where and how to park, including hills.

narration.text: This lesson covers two low-speed skills that still cause plenty of crashes: backing up and parking. You will learn how far and how fast to back, how to look while you do it, and what to do instead of backing if you miss an exit. Then the lesson covers your responsibility when parking, the places where parking is not allowed, how to park on level ground, and the three wheel positions for parking on a hill. The hill rules are a favorite test topic, so the lesson spends extra time on the one case that turns the wheels the other way.

lines.text: No faster than a slow walk.
Turn and look back; use a helper.

narration.text: Because it is hard to see behind a vehicle, back up as little as possible and no faster than a slow walk. When backing, do not rely only on your mirrors and backup camera. Turn your body, look over your right shoulder through the rear window, and use a helper outside the car when you can. After backing, scan left and right before rejoining traffic. A child or a low object can be invisible in mirrors and cameras alike, so a slow speed and your own eyes through the rear window are your best protection whenever you back up.

title.text: Never back up on the road

lines.text: Go on to the next and come back.

narration.text: If you miss an exit or turn, never back up. Continue to the next exit or a safe place to turn, and come back. Backing up on a road or highway puts you against the flow of traffic, where drivers behind you do not expect a vehicle moving toward them. It is tempting when the exit is only a short distance behind you, but those few seconds of reversing are far more dangerous than the few minutes it takes to loop back. Plan your route ahead and watch for exit signs early, so missing a turn happens less often in the first place.

lines.text: Park on the far right, clear of lanes.
No yellow curbs, hydrants, no-parking zones.
Level ground: Park or gear, brake set.

narration.text: You are responsible for making sure your parked vehicle is not a hazard, which normally means parking on the far-right side, clear of any travel lane. Parking is not allowed along yellow-marked curbs, in front of fire hydrants, or where a No Parking sign is posted. Park at a very low speed, and on level ground shift into Park, or into gear with a manual transmission, and set the parking brake. Before you leave the car, check that it is fully out of the lane and that you are not blocking a hydrant, driveway or marked curb, and look for traffic before opening your door.

Hill parking uses the wheels to stop the car from rolling into traffic. Parked uphill with a curb, turn the wheels all the way to the left before shifting into park. Parked uphill without a curb, turn the wheels all the way to the right. Parked downhill, turn the wheels all the way to the right. On any hill, set the emergency brake. The wheel positions point the car toward the curb or the road edge if it does roll, rather than out into the travel lane. Set the wheels before you shift into park so they are in place while you finish parking.

Here is the trap. Three hill cases, and only one goes left. Uphill with a curb is the left-wheel case, while uphill without a curb and every downhill park are right-wheel cases. Learners often remember that the curb matters and then guess for downhill. Downhill is always right, curb or not. So reduce it to one question: am I parked uphill next to a curb? If yes, turn the wheels left. If anything else, turn them right. And in every hill case, set the emergency brake before you walk away from the car. One question settles every hill park.

Here is a quick check: you park uphill on a road with no curb. Which way do the wheels turn? Ask the one question from the trap slide. The answer is all the way to the right. Uphill with a curb is the only left-wheel case; uphill without a curb and every downhill park turn the wheels right. After setting the wheels, shift into park and set the emergency brake, as you should on any hill. If you were parked uphill against a curb instead, the wheels would turn fully to the left before shifting into park. The brake is the final step on any hill.

lines.text: Uphill with curb left; others right.

narration.text: In summary: back up as little as possible, no faster than a slow walk, turning to look through the rear window and using a helper when you can, then scan both ways before rejoining traffic. Never back up for a missed exit or turn. Park on the far right clear of travel lanes, never at yellow curbs, hydrants or no-parking signs, and on level ground use Park or gear plus the parking brake. On hills, uphill with a curb turns the wheels left, all other cases right, and the emergency brake is always set. Practice these until they become routine.

why_how.text: Parallel parking is a skills test maneuver, and a set sequence makes it repeatable.
The right distances keep you close to the curb without touching other cars.

scenario.text: Raj starts to parallel park by stopping a full car width away from the car ahead of the space.

reasoning.text: The start position is alongside the vehicle ahead, about two feet away from it.

result.text: Raj moves to about two feet from the car ahead before backing in.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking you should end as far from the curb as you are from the other cars.

correction.text: You end about a foot from the curb, but at least two feet from the vehicles ahead and behind.

prompt.text: While backing into a parallel space, your front bumper has just cleared the car ahead. What do you do next?

answer.text: Turn the wheel sharply the other way and keep backing slowly until you are parallel to the curb.

rationale.text: After your bumper clears the vehicle in front, the sharp opposite turn swings the front of your car in toward the curb.

narration.text: Parallel parking between two vehicles looks hard, but it becomes manageable when you break it into steps. This lesson covers choosing a space, the exact starting position, each steering change as you back in, and the distances to end with. You will be asked to park on the skills test, so it helps to practice each step slowly in a quiet place until the sequence feels automatic. The lesson also points out the two pairs of distances that are easy to mix up, so you can answer questions about them as confidently as you perform the maneuver.

lines.text: Space a few feet longer than your car.
Signal; stop beside the car ahead.

narration.text: For parallel parking between vehicles, watch for traffic, pedestrians and fixed objects, and look for a space about three to six feet longer than your vehicle. Parallel parking starts with your turn signal on and a stop alongside the vehicle ahead of the space, about two feet away from it. The signal tells drivers behind you that you are about to back up, so they leave you room. Line up so your car is roughly even with the vehicle ahead, and check your mirrors and over your shoulder for traffic before you begin to back.

lines.text: Turn the wheel fully toward your side.
Straighten as your door passes their bumper.

narration.text: Next, turn the wheel fully toward the side you are parking on, left for the left side of the road and right for the right side, and back up slowly. When your front door passes the rear bumper of the car you are parking behind, straighten the wheel and keep backing slowly in a straight line. That straight section brings your rear wheels close to the curb before the final swing. Keep looking back through the rear window and glancing at your mirrors, and stop at once if a pedestrian or another vehicle moves into your path.

lines.text: Bumper clears the car in front?

narration.text: Once your bumper clears the vehicle in front, turn the wheel sharply the other way and back slowly until you are parallel to the curb. This swings the front of your car into the space. Finish by straightening the wheels, ending about a foot from the curb and at least two feet from the vehicles ahead and behind. If you end up too far from the curb or too close to another car, it is fine to pull forward and adjust. A careful correction is always better than bumping another vehicle, and practice will reduce how often you need one.

lines.text: Start: about two feet beside the car ahead.
Space: three to six feet longer.
End: a foot from curb, two from cars.

narration.text: Here is the trap: several distances in one maneuver. When you begin parallel parking you stop about two feet from the car ahead, and the space you choose should be about three to six feet longer than your car. At the end you should be about a foot from the curb, but at least two feet from the vehicles ahead and behind. People swap the foot and the two feet at the end most often. Remember that the curb gets the closest distance, a foot, while the other cars get more room, at least two feet each. The curb gets the closest distance.

lines.text: Bumper clears the car ahead: then?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: while backing into a parallel space, your front bumper has just cleared the car ahead. What do you do next? Think through the sequence. You turn the wheel sharply the other way and keep backing slowly until you are parallel to the curb. After your bumper clears the vehicle in front, that sharp opposite turn swings the front of your car in toward the curb. Then you straighten the wheels and check that you are about a foot from the curb and at least two feet from the vehicles ahead and behind. Each step sets up the next.

lines.text: Signal, stop beside, back and turn.

narration.text: To wrap up: look for a space about three to six feet longer than your car and watch for traffic, pedestrians and objects. Signal and stop beside the vehicle ahead, about two feet away. Turn the wheel fully toward your parking side and back slowly. Straighten when your front door passes the other car's rear bumper, then turn sharply the other way once your bumper clears the car in front, and back until parallel. Finish with straight wheels about a foot from the curb and at least two feet from the vehicles around you.

why_how.text: Other drivers can only react to what they can see and hear, so your lights, signals and horn are how you communicate.
Headlight rules make sure you can see and be seen in every condition.

scenario.text: Cam drives on a gray afternoon in light rain with the wipers on and no headlights.

reasoning.text: Low beams are recommended whenever the wipers are on and in rain, snow or fog.

result.text: Cam switches on the low beams.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking low beams are only required in full darkness.

correction.text: Low beams are required from a half hour after sunset and whenever you cannot see a vehicle or person five hundred feet away.

memory_support.text: Tap to alert, press to warn.

prompt.text: It is twenty minutes after sunset and still fairly light. Are low beams required yet?

answer.text: Not by the time rule until a half hour after sunset, unless visibility is under five hundred feet.

rationale.text: Low beams are required from a half hour after sunset to a half hour before sunrise, and any time you cannot see five hundred feet.

narration.text: This lesson is about how you communicate with other road users and how you see and are seen. You will learn the tools for letting others know where you are and what you plan, why strong emotions are a reason not to drive, and the two different uses of the horn. Then the lesson covers headlights in detail: why low beams matter even with automatic lights, when they are required and when they are only recommended, when to use high beams, how to handle another driver's glare, and what parking lights are for. Clear communication prevents many crashes.

Let other drivers know where you are and what you intend by using headlights, brakes, turn signals and hazard lights, and by keeping space ahead and behind. Space is a message too: a steady gap tells others you are in control. Strong emotions affect safe driving, so do not drive when you are very worried, excited, afraid, angry or depressed. A driver in that state is slower to notice hazards and more likely to take risks. If you feel that way, wait until you are calm or ask someone else to drive, even if it means arriving later than planned.

lines.text: Hard press: warn of a collision.

narration.text: The horn exists to help prevent crashes. A light tap gets another driver's attention, for example when someone starts to back out without seeing you. A hard press warns of a collision about to happen. Using the horn for anything else, such as expressing frustration, weakens its value as a warning and can startle other drivers into mistakes. Keep it for its two safety jobs. When you do use it, keep your foot ready on the brake, because the other driver may not respond the way you hope. Used well, the horn is a safety tool, not a complaint, and a short tap is usually enough to be noticed.

lines.text: Help you see and be seen.

narration.text: Low beams help you see and be seen. Even if your car switches them on automatically, learn the manual control and check that they come on when needed. Low beams are required when you cannot see a vehicle or person five hundred feet away, about one block, and from a half hour after sunset to a half hour before sunrise. Low beams are recommended whenever your windshield wipers are on and in rain, snow or fog. Using them in those conditions makes your car far easier for others to spot, even in daylight, when gray weather hides a car without lights.

lines.text: Required: five hundred feet; sunset rule.
Recommended: wipers on; rain, snow, fog.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Low beams are required at the five hundred foot visibility threshold and in the half hour after sunset through the half hour before sunrise, but they are only recommended with wipers on or in rain, snow or fog. Test questions like to blur those two lists. If the question is about what the law requires, look for the visibility threshold or the time around sunset and sunrise. If it is about weather or wipers, the word is recommended. In practice, follow both: there is no downside to turning on low beams whenever you are unsure.

lines.text: Glare: look right. Parking lights: parked.

narration.text: High beams let you see twice as far as low beams. Use them when no vehicles are approaching or in an unfamiliar place or construction area, and dim them for oncoming traffic. If an oncoming driver leaves the high beams on, look toward the right side of the road rather than into the glare. Use parking lights only while parked and idling; they are not a substitute for headlights while driving. So high beams are for open, empty roads, low beams for everything else while moving, and parking lights only when the car is stopped.

Here is a quick check: it is twenty minutes after sunset and still fairly light. Are low beams required yet? Apply both parts of the rule. By the time rule, not until a half hour after sunset, unless you cannot see a vehicle or person five hundred feet away, in which case they are required now. Low beams are required from a half hour after sunset to a half hour before sunrise, and any time visibility is under five hundred feet. Many drivers simply switch them on early, which is a safe habit that the rules never forbid.

lines.text: Tap to alert; press to warn.

narration.text: In summary: show your plans with lights, brakes, signals, hazards and space, and do not drive when very upset or excited. A light horn tap gets attention, and a hard press warns of an imminent collision. Learn your manual low-beam control. Low beams are required when you cannot see five hundred feet and from a half hour after sunset to a half hour before sunrise, and recommended with wipers on or in rain, snow or fog. Use high beams on empty roads, dim them for oncoming traffic, look right to avoid glare, and keep parking lights for when you are parked.

why_how.text: Signals tell others what you will do before you do it, which gives them time to react.
Hand signals keep you communicating when turn signals fail.

scenario.text: Ana plans to turn right into a gas station just past an intersection and signals before reaching the intersection.

reasoning.text: For a turn just after an intersection, wait until you have crossed the intersection before signaling.

result.text: Ana crosses the intersection first, then signals for the gas station.

claim.text: Common mistake: signaling before an intersection for a turn that comes just after it.

correction.text: Wait until you have crossed the intersection, so drivers there do not think you are turning at the corner.

memory_support.text: Signal, check, move; three seconds early.

prompt.text: Your turn signals stop working. How do you signal a right turn by hand?

answer.text: Hold your arm out the driver window with the elbow bent and the hand pointing up.

rationale.text: Straight arm means left, bent upward means right, and pointed down means slowing or stopping.

narration.text: This short lesson finishes the basics with signaling. You will learn the order in which to signal, check and move, how early to signal before a turn at an intersection, and the important exception when your turn comes just after an intersection. Then you will learn the three hand signals that can replace turn signals that are missing or hard to see. Signals are how you tell other drivers what you are about to do, so getting the timing right is just as important as remembering to signal at all. Good timing makes every signal useful.

lines.text: About three seconds before an intersection turn.

narration.text: The order is simple: turn on your signal, check around you, and then move. At an intersection, begin signaling about three seconds, roughly one hundred feet, before the turn. That gives drivers behind you time to slow down and gives oncoming drivers and pedestrians a clear message about where you are going. Signaling too late, as you are already turning, gives no useful warning. Signaling far too early can mislead others into thinking you will turn at an earlier street or driveway, so aim for that roughly three-second window.

lines.text: Cross the intersection first, then signal.

narration.text: Here is the trap. When your turn comes just after an intersection, such as a driveway on the far side, signaling before the intersection makes other drivers think you are turning at the corner. A driver waiting to pull out may move into your path. So the rule changes: wait until you have crossed the intersection before signaling. At a normal intersection turn you signal about three seconds, roughly one hundred feet, ahead of the turn, but for a turn just past an intersection you wait until you have crossed it, then signal for your turn.

lines.text: Slow or stop: hand pointed down.

narration.text: Hand signals may replace turn signals that are missing or hard to see, for example if a signal bulb has burned out. To turn left, hold your arm straight out the driver window. To turn right, bend your elbow with the hand pointing up. To slow or stop, point your hand down. All three are given with the left arm from the driver window, so the position of the arm is what carries the meaning. Practice them before you need them, and remember that a working turn signal is still the clearest message when it is available. Know all three before you need them.

lines.text: Signals broken: how to show right?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: your turn signals stop working. How do you signal a right turn by hand? Picture the three arm positions. You hold your arm out the driver window with the elbow bent and the hand pointing up. In hand signals a straight arm means a left turn, an arm bent upward means a right turn, and an arm pointed down means slowing or stopping. Give the signal early, about the same three seconds before the turn as you would with your turn signal, and get the broken signal repaired as soon as you can. A good signal is clear and early.

lines.text: Signal, check, move; three seconds early.
Straight left, bent up right, down stop.

narration.text: To finish: turn on your signal, check around you, then move. At an intersection, start signaling about three seconds, roughly one hundred feet, before the turn. When your turn comes just after an intersection, wait until you have crossed it before signaling. If your turn signals are missing or hard to see, use hand signals: arm straight out for a left turn, elbow bent with the hand up for a right turn, and hand pointed down to slow or stop. That completes the basics; next you will move on to the signs chapter of the handbook.
